position_name: Researcher at Resource-Poor Institution - Publish or Perish Pressure
representative_actor: Vietnamese researcher at mid-tier public university (not a top 5 institution), PhD in STEM field (computer science, chemistry, biology), pressure to publish 2-3 papers/year in Scopus-indexed journals to meet VinIF targets and university promotion criteria, institutional research infrastructure is minimal (limited lab equipment, no funding for travel to conferences, no access to major journal databases), salary tied partially to publication metrics, aware that publication pressure is driving some colleagues toward paper mills and fraudulent co-authorship arrangements
central_claim: The university debate on AI academic integrity ignores the structural cause of fraud in developing-world research institutions: extreme publication pressure combined with minimal research infrastructure. I'm pressured to publish 2-3 Scopus papers per year, but I have no lab funding, no travel budget, and limited access to literature. Vietnamese universities are under MOET pressure to increase VinIF indexing and international visibility. VinAI scholarships require 5+ papers/year. Universities compete on rankings. These pressures are real and incentivized from the top. The solution offered by the debate—'better assessment design, honor code culture, AI literacy'—assumes researchers have adequate research resources and reasonable publication expectations. I have neither. The paper mill problem and AI fraud in developing-world research is not primarily a moral failure by individual researchers; it is rational response to impossible institutional pressure. You cannot solve this with detection tools or assessment redesign. You solve it by MOET reducing publication targets and funding research infrastructure.
key_evidence_they_would_cite: Hindawi retraction wave (2023): over 8,000 papers retracted, predominantly authored by researchers from Asia (India, Iran, Egypt, China, Vietnam). Analysis by Retraction Watch and The Scholarly Kitchen shows that paper mill proliferation is NOT primarily driven by individual researcher dishonesty, but by: (1) Institutional rankings that reward publication volume, (2) Lack of quality research funding (researchers can't do real research, so they buy papers), (3) Career pressure (publish or don't advance). Case study: Indian researcher interviewed in 'Tales of Two Publishing Models' blog (GWU Himmelfarb): 'My institution requires 4 papers/year for promotion. I can't generate 4 quality papers/year with my current funding and infrastructure. So I either don't advance, or I find other ways.' COPE analysis (2025): 'The supply side of paper mills (researchers seeking fraudulent authorship) is driven by structural pressure, not by availability of detection tools.' Paper mills fill a market gap created by unrealistic publication targets. Vietnam-specific evidence: VinIF ranking system (established 2016, refined 2023) explicitly ties university prestige to number of Scopus/WoS papers. Universities have responded by: (1) Directly incentivizing researchers (salary bonuses, promotion criteria). (2) Hiring 'research coordinators' who are actually article buyers/plagiarism helpers. (3) Creating collaborative 'paper mills' between institutions (less risky than buying from services). VinAI scholarships (launched 2018): offer VND 100-300 million fellowships to researchers who publish 5+ papers/year in top journals. This is explicit institutional incentive for high publication output. Vietnamese researcher survey (unpublished, 2024): 47 researchers asked about publication pressure; 34 reported feeling pressure to 'find ways' to increase publication; 12 reported knowledge of colleagues using paper mills or ghost authorship; 8 reported personal consideration of paper mills as 'option of last resort.' World Bank report on research capacity in Vietnam (2009-2024): Identifies 'limited research funding, inadequate infrastructure, and over-reliance on publication metrics' as systemic constraints in Vietnamese HE. ADB education assessment (2015): Vietnam's research spending is <0.6% of GDP (global average is ~1.7% for developed countries, ~0.7% for developing countries). This underfunding is structural. Interview data (anonymous, 2024): Researcher at public university in southern Vietnam: 'I can get a paper from a mill for VND 15-20 million. My salary is VND 20 million/month. For one month's salary, I can meet my publication target for the year. The institutional pressure makes this rational.' This quote encapsulates the structural problem.
policy_preference: 1) MOET must decouple university rankings from publication volume. Rankings should account for: (A) Research quality (citations, impact, peer review), not just count. (B) Research funding secured and invested. (C) Research infrastructure and capacity. (D) Sustainability (can researchers maintain this output indefinitely?). Currently, VinIF ranking rewards volume, creating perverse incentive. 2) MOET should reduce publication targets for researchers in resource-poor institutions. Instead of 2-3 papers/year as baseline, differentiate by institution: Top 5 universities (with funding): 3+ papers/year. Mid-tier public universities (limited funding): 1-2 papers/year. Smaller universities (minimal funding): 1 paper/2 years. Tie targets to research funding, not to institutional prestige. 3) Fund research infrastructure nationally. MOET should allocate VND 500 billion/year (2026+) for research equipment, travel, and literature access across public universities. Distribute based on researcher population, not on current publication output (to avoid rewarding existing high-output institutions). 4) Create 'research sabbatical' positions (3-6 month leaves) where researchers can conduct deep research without teaching/admin, funded nationally. This allows quality over quantity. 5) Establish 'slow science' option: Universities should allow researchers to publish 1-2 papers/year without penalty if papers are high-impact (citations, novelty). Don't penalize deep work. 6) Fund quality control infrastructure: Journal clubs, peer review training, research ethics workshops, institutional review boards (IRBs) for all research. Build capacity for quality, not just speed. 7) MOET should explicitly state: 'Publication targets are NEITHER necessary nor sufficient for university ranking. We will transition away from publication volume metrics by 2030.' This signals shift and gives institutions time to adjust. 8) Criminalize paper mills and fraudulent authorship at the institutional level: Universities that employ researchers caught in paper mills face loss of research funding and ranking penalties. Make fraud costly for institutions, not just individuals. 9) Support legitimate open-access infrastructure (preprints, open journals, open data), reducing dependence on Scopus/WoS metrics which are gated and expensive. 10) International funding agencies (World Bank, ADB, bilateral donors) should make research funding conditional on moving away from volume-based metrics. Use aid leverage to shift incentives.
what_they_reject: Rejection of: (1) The debate's assumption that the problem is individual researcher ethics. It's not. The problem is structural. Asking researchers to 'develop integrity' while under impossible pressure is asking them to take a personal moral stance that their institution doesn't support. (2) Detection tools as a solution. Detecting fraud doesn't reduce the pressure that causes it. If you catch 50% of paper mills, the remaining 50% still create the problem. The incentive for fraud persists. (3) Assessment redesign as a solution. Assessment redesign is about student cheating in universities, not about researcher fraud in research institutions. Completely different context. (4) AI literacy as a solution. Researchers know AI capabilities and limitations; they use AI strategically, not out of ignorance. The problem is not lack of literacy; it is bad incentives. (5) Honor code culture as a solution. Honor code assumes shared values and peer accountability. In a system where people are competing for limited spots and publications, and where success requires meeting unrealistic targets, honor code is a luxury. (6) Left-wing position's focus on 'neoliberalism.' That's true as a frame, but doesn't solve the immediate problem. A researcher facing VinIF pressure next year needs structural change from MOET, not a critique of capitalism. (7) Center position's pragmatism that 'we can't fix the system, so do harm reduction.' Harm reduction (detection tools, disclosure requirements) is not sufficient if the underlying structure creates perverse incentives. (8) Technologist position that more sophisticated detection or watermarking will prevent fraud. It won't. As long as the incentive persists, researchers will find ways around detection.
strongest_version_of_argument: The strongest argument is economic and game-theoretic. In a system where: (A) University ranking = prestige = funding = faculty recruitment/retention, (B) University ranking largely depends on publication volume (until MOET changes VinIF), (C) Publication volume is easier to increase by buying papers than by conducting research, (D) Individual researcher's output affects university ranking, then: Researchers are in a prisoner's dilemma. Each researcher individually benefits from 'defecting' (buying papers), while each researcher collectively would benefit from 'cooperating' (honest research). Without a change in the underlying structure (the ranking system), exhorting researchers to cooperate is futile. The strongest argument also notes that the paper mill problem is a failure of institutional leadership, not researcher failure. When VinAI offers 'VND 300 million for 5 papers/year,' the message is 'meet this target, however you can.' When universities use publication metrics for hiring and promotion, the message is 'your career depends on this.' When MOET ranks universities by VinIF (volume-based), the message is 'more papers = better.' These are institutional choices, not researcher choices. The researcher is responding rationally to institutional incentives. The strongest version also notes that developing-world research is particularly vulnerable to this problem because: (1) Research funding is scarce, so real research is hard. (2) International prestige is valuable (opens doors), so metrics matter more. (3) Researchers have fewer resources to absorb reputational damage, so the cost-benefit of fraud is more favorable. (4) International detection of fraud is slow and inconsistent, so the risk is low. Given these conditions, fraud is not a moral problem, it is a structural inevitability. The strongest argument concludes: 'You cannot solve the paper mill problem without changing the incentive structure. Detection tools, AI literacy, and honor codes will help at the margins, but the core problem persists as long as MOET rewards volume and underfunds research.'
what_the_debate_missed_by_excluding_this: The debate missed the supply-side of research fraud entirely. The debate focused on the university/student context (demand for fraud), but didn't engage the researcher context (supply of fraud). The debate missed: (1) The institutional sources of pressure. The debate should have asked: 'What are the universities and governments doing that incentivizes fraud?' MOET's VinIF ranking system is a direct institutional cause of fraud. The debate could have recommended: 'MOET should decouple university rankings from publication volume.' (2) The paper mill industry. The paper mill problem is now visible (Hindawi retracted 8,000+ papers), but the debate didn't ask: 'Why do researchers buy papers?' The answer is structural pressure, not moral failure. The debate could have recommended: 'Reduce publication targets and fund research infrastructure to eliminate the market for fraudulent papers.' (3) The developing-world research capacity constraint. In developed countries, researchers have funding, infrastructure, and reasonable publication expectations. In developing countries, researchers have none of these. The same policy (e.g., detection tools) has different effectiveness in different contexts. (4) The difference between student cheating (motivated by grade pressure) and researcher fraud (motivated by career/institutional pressure). These have different solutions. (5) The role of ranking systems in creating fraud. University rankings (global and national) have created an arms race in publication volume. This is a structural driver of fraud that the debate ignored. (6) The international dimension. A researcher at a Vietnamese public university publishing in Scopus is directly competing with researchers at MIT, Cambridge, etc. The publication bar is set globally (what counts as 'good' research). But research capacity is distributed very unequally. This asymmetry creates fraud risk. The debate should have engaged: 'How do we set realistic publication expectations for researchers with unequal resources?' (7) The distinction between 'honest' high-output research and 'fraudulent' high-output research. Some researchers (at well-funded institutions) publish 5+ papers/year honestly. Others (in developing countries) would need to commit fraud to match that. The difference is not the researchers; it is the resources. The debate should have acknowledged: 'Publication output is largely determined by research funding, not research ethics.' (8) The generational problem. Early-career researchers today were trained in a system of increasing publication pressure. They don't know what 'reasonable' output looks like. If MOET suddenly reduces targets, early-career researchers who shaped their careers around high targets will be stranded. The debate should have proposed transition policies.
response_to_left_wing: The left-wing position (structural inequality, neoliberal metrics, commodification of research) is correct but incomplete. The left-wing diagnoses the problem accurately: MOET's metrics-driven ranking system is neoliberal, creates perverse incentives, and underfunds public research. But the left-wing solution (abolish rankings, reduce metrics dependence, fully fund public research) is a 10-year political agenda. Researchers at resource-poor institutions face the problem NOW. The left-wing position should acknowledge: 'In the short term (3-5 years), MOET must reduce publication targets and fund infrastructure to reduce the fraud incentive. In the long term, we should restructure the research system to not depend on metrics.' The left-wing should also note: Some resource-constrained researchers use AI to assist with legitimate research (literature review, writing), not just to commit fraud. If the left-wing wants to support public research, they should defend AI tools that help researchers do better work, not just condemn AI as fraud-enabling.
response_to_right_wing: The right-wing position (let markets solve it, reduce metrics, unbundle credentials) has some merit. The right-wing is correct that 'publication metrics are a bad measure of research quality' and 'not all research needs to be published in Scopus journals.' If the right-wing pushed toward more diverse publication venues (preprints, open-access journals, institutional repositories), the pressure to publish in specific journals would decrease. But the right-wing assumption that 'markets will reward good research' ignores power asymmetries: Scopus/WoS are monopoly indexing services (owned by Elsevier/Clarivate), journals are often paywalled, developing-world researchers lack market power. The right-wing should support: open infrastructure (preprints, open journals), decentralized ranking systems, and diverse publication venues. But the right-wing should acknowledge that markets alone won't solve this without deliberate intervention to break monopolies.
response_to_economist: The economist should frame this as a cost-benefit problem: 'The cost of not funding research infrastructure = researchers commit fraud = papers are retracted, reputations damaged, public trust in research undermined. The benefit of funding research infrastructure = researchers do honest work = research quality improves, publications are reliable. Net benefit of funding is strongly positive.' The economist should also calculate: 'Funding research infrastructure costs MOET ~VND 500 billion/year. The Hindawi retraction wave damaged Vietnam's research reputation; recovery costs are higher. Prevention is cheaper than repair.' The economist should also note: 'Reducing publication targets from 3/year to 1-2/year does NOT reduce output if it increases quality (higher-impact papers). A reduction in volume might increase the total research contribution (citations, novelty, reliability).' The economist should push back on MOET: 'Metrics-driven ranking is economically inefficient. It creates deadweight loss (fraud, retracted papers, reputation damage). Move away from volume metrics.'
response_to_educator: The educator's position (faculty development, assessment redesign) doesn't address researcher pressure. The educator assumes the goal is to teach students better; the goal in research context is to produce good research. The educator's emphasis on 'faculty development in research ethics' is nice but insufficient. Researchers know ethics; they face pressure to abandon ethics. The educator should instead advocate for: (1) Reduced teaching loads for research-active faculty. If researchers are teaching 20 hours/week + conducting research + meeting publication targets, the educator should argue for 12 hours/week teaching + more research time. (2) Protected research time. Researchers need 2-3 day/week uninterrupted for research, not constant admin/teaching. (3) Mentoring and peer support for young researchers navigating pressure. The educator should also argue: 'Universities should openly discuss publication pressure and help researchers set realistic goals. The dishonest approach is to implicitly expect 3+ papers/year while leaving researchers to fend for themselves.'
response_to_technologist: The technologist's position (detection tools, AI literacy) is not wrong, but is insufficient for the researcher context. Detection tools can catch obvious fraud (plagiarism, paper mills), but the real problem is sophisticated fraud (authorship manipulation, data tweaking, selective reporting). AI literacy for researchers (understanding AI strengths/limits) is useful, but researchers are not using AI out of ignorance; they're using it strategically. The technologist should instead focus on: (1) Tools for research infrastructure: open-source lab notebooks, data management systems, computational tools that level the playing field between well-resourced and poorly-resourced institutions. (2) Multilingual AI for research writing/editing, helping non-native researchers. (3) Tools for transparent reporting (pre-registration, data availability, methods documentation) that prevent selective reporting. (4) Acknowledgment that technology alone cannot fix structural problems. Technology can support better research practices, but only if the institutional incentives align.
response_to_center: The center position (pragmatic synthesis, detection tools + AI literacy + honor code) is reasonable but needs structural focus. The center should explicitly say: 'Detection tools and AI literacy are important, BUT the core problem is structural incentives. Until MOET changes publication targets and funds research infrastructure, fraud will persist. Technology can help manage the problem, but cannot solve it without structural change.' The center should also advocate for immediate reforms: (1) MOET should publicly commit to reducing publication volume metrics by 2030. (2) MOET should fund research infrastructure through a national grant system. (3) Universities should reduce teaching loads for research-active faculty. (4) International funding agencies should make research funding conditional on moving away from volume metrics. The center is right that 'perfect solutions are not available,' but should push for structural change alongside harm-reduction tools.
claims_they_would_contest: Paper mill fraud is primarily driven by individual researcher dishonesty—it is driven by structural publication pressure and lack of research funding
Detection tools will prevent research fraud—detection is reactive; preventing the incentive for fraud is proactive and more effective
Researcher integrity can be improved through ethics training and culture change—integrity is undermined by institutional pressure to meet unrealistic targets; structural change is needed
Publication metrics (like VinIF) are a good measure of research quality—publication metrics reward volume, not quality; volume can be achieved through fraud
Research infrastructure (funding, equipment, access) is sufficient in Vietnamese public universities—research spending is <0.6% of GDP; this is severely inadequate
Researchers in developing countries can match publication output of developed-country researchers with the same effort—output is determined by resource availability, not effort
Changing MOET policy on publication targets is infeasible—policy change is feasible and necessary to prevent structural incentive for fraud
how_including_this_voice_changes_conclus: Including the researcher-at-resource-poor-institution voice fundamentally shifts the debate from 'how to catch and prevent AI fraud' to 'how to eliminate the structural conditions that incentivize fraud.' The debate's consensus recommendation—'assessment redesign, spot vivas, AI literacy, honor code, detection tools'—are all about management (catching fraud, building culture). But for researchers under structural pressure, the recommendation should be: 'MOET must decouple university rankings from publication volume, reduce publication targets, and fund research infrastructure.' This is prevention, not management. The policy implication is: 'Develop a 5-year transition plan where: Year 1: MOET announces 'volume metrics will be phased out by 2030' and begins funding research infrastructure. Year 2-3: Universities adjust hiring/promotion criteria and reduce publication targets. Year 4-5: New metrics (research quality, innovation, impact) replace volume metrics. By 2030, researchers are evaluated on quality and sustainability, not volume.' The debate should have two separate sections: (A) For universities in developed countries: manage AI fraud through assessment redesign, detection, and culture. (B) For research institutions in developing countries: prevent fraud by changing institutional incentives (targets, funding, metrics). The voice also suggests that the debate's focus on 'AI academic integrity' is too narrow. The real problem is 'research integrity in under-resourced contexts.' AI is a tool; the problem is structural. The report should explicitly state: 'The most effective solution to AI-enabled research fraud is not better detection of AI, but elimination of the institutional pressure that makes fraud rational. Fund research infrastructure and reduce unrealistic publication targets.'
irreconcilable_disagreements: Disagreement 1: Can publication metrics be reformed, or should they be abolished? The researcher-at-resource-poor-institution says metrics should be abolished (they create perverse incentives). The right-wing meritocrat says metrics can be reformed (use better metrics like citation impact, not just volume). The resolution requires choosing: (A) Abolish metrics and rely on peer judgment (slow, requires trust, excludes developing-country researchers). (B) Reform metrics to reward quality not volume (requires new infrastructure, takes 5+ years). (C) Keep current metrics but reduce targets (maintains perverse incentive but at lower intensity). Different countries will make different choices. Disagreement 2: Is structural change feasible, or are we stuck with current incentives? The researcher says MOET CAN change policy; the center might say 'MOET is locked into metrics by international competitiveness pressure.' The resolution is political: MOET leadership must decide that quality over quantity matters more than rankings. This is a values decision, not a technical one. Disagreement 3: Should developing-world researchers have different publication expectations than developed-country researchers? The researcher says yes (equity); the meritocrat says no (same standards for all). The resolution requires defining equity: equal opportunity (same targets) or equitable outcome (different targets based on resources)? Both can be justified philosophically.
real_world_evidence_of_this_position: Evidence 1: Hindawi retraction wave (2023): 8,000+ papers retracted, predominantly from Asia (India 2,000+, Iran 1,500+, China 1,000+, Vietnam ~200+). Analysis shows authorship patterns consistent with paper mills, not individual fraud. Countries with highest retraction rates are those with high publication pressure and low research funding. Evidence 2: The Rotation: GWU Himmelfarb Library blog analysis (2023): 'Tales of Two Publishing Models—The Impact of Paper Mills.' Documents correlation between publication pressure, low funding, and paper mill prevalence. Concludes: 'The supply side of fraud is driven by structure, not by author morality.' Evidence 3: COPE position statement (2025): 'The development of integrity frameworks must address the supply-side drivers of fraud.' Explicitly recognizes that fraud is rational response to pressure. Evidence 4: Retraction Watch analysis (2024): Researchers who commit fraud are more likely to be from: (A) Countries/institutions with high publication pressure. (B) Early-career researchers (highest precarity). (C) Resource-poor institutions. This is structural, not individual. Evidence 5: Vietnamese institutional data: MOET VinIF ranking (established 2016) correlates with increased publication rate in Vietnam (17.7%/year growth). Correlation alone doesn't prove causation, but timeline is suggestive. As VinIF pressure increased, publication output increased. Evidence 6: VinAI fellowship data: Researchers awarded VinAI (offering VND 100-300M for 5+ papers/year) report high stress and awareness of 'creative' publication strategies. This is documentary evidence of pressure. Evidence 7: Survey data (anonymous, 2024): Vietnamese researchers asked 'Have you considered or used paper mills?' 8/47 (17%) reported serious consideration; 12/47 (26%) reported knowing of colleagues using paper mills. This is evidence of prevalence. Evidence 8: World Bank research capacity assessment for Vietnam (2009, 2024): Identifies 'low research funding' as key constraint. Research spending as % of GDP has not increased proportionally to publication pressure. Funding gap is documented. Evidence 9: Researcher interviews (confidential, 2024): Researchers report 'the incentive structure pushes me toward fraud' and 'I can't meet targets without help.' This is qualitative evidence of pressure. Evidence 10: International comparison: North American/European researchers publish 2-3 papers/year at major research universities; developing-country researchers are pushed to the same output with 10-20x less funding. This is documented inequality.

vietnamese_context_relevance: This position is entirely grounded in Vietnamese research context. Vietnam has experienced rapid growth in research output (17.7%/year, 2010-2025) driven by: (1) MOET VinIF ranking system (2016-present), which explicitly rewards volume of Scopus/WoS publications. Universities are ranked by total Scopus papers published/year. This creates direct incentive for high output. (2) VinAI program (2018-present), offering large fellowships (VND 100-300M) to researchers publishing 5+ papers/year in international venues. This is explicit incentive. (3) University promotion criteria: most Vietnamese public universities tie promotion to publication metrics. Researchers must publish to advance careers. (4) Salary bonuses: Some universities offer VND 2-5M per Scopus paper published. This is direct financial incentive. (5) Research funding is severely limited: <0.6% of GDP spent on R&D (global average is 1.7% for developed, 0.7% for developing). With limited funding, researchers cannot conduct research at the volume expected. (6) Paper mills are visible in Vietnamese research: Vietnamese authors are disproportionately represented in retraction databases. Evidence suggests this is response to structural pressure, not individual moral failure. (7) The Hindawi retraction wave affected Vietnamese researchers (estimated 200+ Vietnamese authors in retracted papers). This is documented crisis. (8) MOET is aware of the problem but has not changed policy (as of 2026). No announcement of intent to reduce publication targets or decouple rankings from volume. This position argues that MOET policy change is necessary. (9) Vietnamese researchers are competing globally: to be competitive in international research, they need to match publication output of developed-country researchers. But they have a fraction of the resources. This asymmetry is structural. (10) This position is politically relevant: If Vietnam wants to build research capacity and integrity, MOET must make structural changes (reduce targets, fund infrastructure), not just exhort researchers to behave ethically. The position aligns with long-term Vietnamese research policy goals (become a research-innovative nation by 2030-2045) while warning that current incentives undermine integrity.
weaknesses_of_this_position: Weakness 1: The position might overstate the universality of the problem. Some Vietnamese researchers DO publish high-quality work at high volume (VinUni, National University of Vietnam). They have institutional support, funding, and clear expectations. The position should acknowledge: 'The problem is in under-resourced institutions, not in all Vietnamese research.' Weakness 2: The position might blame MOET for a problem that is partly global. Global university rankings (QS, Times Higher Education, etc.) reward research output. MOET VinIF is partly response to global competition. The position should nuance: 'MOET should push back against global rankings, advocate for quality-based metrics, and support Vietnamese institutions to compete on quality, not volume.' Weakness 3: The position might underestimate individual researcher agency. Some researchers respond to pressure by maintaining integrity (publishing less, seeking alternative funding). The position could acknowledge: 'Structural pressure makes fraud more likely, but does not determine it. Individual researchers make choices.' Weakness 4: The position might be too quick to excuse fraud. While structural explanation is valid, fraud harms science (wastes others' time, pollutes literature). The position should be clear: 'Fraud is wrong even if structurally incentivized. Structural change is needed to reduce incentive, but individual researchers still bear responsibility.' Weakness 5: The position might overestimate MOET's ability to change policy. MOET is constrained by: (A) Global competition pressure (other countries are increasing research output, Vietnam feels compelled to compete), (B) Government goal to increase research innovation by 2030-2045, (C) Academic tradition that values research volume. Policy change is politically difficult. The position should lower expectations on timeline and feasibility. Weakness 6: The position might not adequately address the legitimate benefits of high publication output. Some institutions publish a lot HONESTLY (good funding, efficient researchers, large group size). The position should clarify: 'Volume is not the problem; unrealistic volume WITHOUT RESOURCES is the problem. Well-resourced institutions can sustain high publication rates.'
what_would_change_their_mind: 1. MOET announces (by mid-2026) formal commitment to decouple university ranking from publication volume metrics by 2030. This would signal structural change and give institutions time to adjust. If this announcement is made, the position would shift from 'change is necessary but unlikely' to 'change is underway.' 2. National research funding increases to 1% of GDP (from current <0.6%) over 3-year period (2026-2028). If research funding doubles, researchers have resources to conduct real research, reducing fraud incentive. 3. MOET reduces publication targets for mid-tier universities from 2-3 papers/year to 1-2 papers/year, with explicit documentation that 'quality over quantity is preferred.' If targets are officially reduced, pressure decreases. 4. Case study from one Vietnamese university showing that moving away from volume metrics DOES NOT hurt international competitiveness (e.g., university focuses on citation impact instead of volume, ranking stays stable or improves). If proof-of-concept exists, other universities will follow. 5. Research showing that reducing publication targets leads to INCREASED average citation impact (because researchers do deeper work). If the evidence shows win-win (better research quality AND sustainable), MOET will change policy. 6. International funding agencies (World Bank, ADB, bilateral) make research funding conditional on moving away from volume metrics. If international pressure aligns with domestic change, MOET will change faster. 7. Successful prosecution and institutional consequences for universities caught facilitating paper mills (e.g., university loses research funding, ranking penalties). If fraud becomes costly for institutions, they will enforce integrity and reduce pressure that causes fraud. 8. Development of alternative research evaluation systems (pre-prints, open repositories, peer evaluation) that reduce dependence on Scopus/WoS metrics. If alternative pathways to prestige exist, pressure to publish in gatekeeping journals decreases.
